That approach can generate local wins but it rarely transforms how a business creates value.
L76: 
L77: It is akin to creating interactive banners and drip email campaigns with the arrival of the internet, and missing the point of the eCommerce revolution.
L78: The organizations pulling ahead use a different, and more ambitious logic. They treat AI not as a collection of disconnected experiments, but as a portfolio of value models. Each has its own economics, time-to-value, and governance requirements, and each makes the next one easier to scale.
L79: This is why the companies that get the most from AI will not be the ones running the most pilots. They will be the ones that understand which value models to build, in what sequence, and with what foundations to reinvent their own business.
L80: ## From pilots to portfolios
L81: 
L82: There are five AI value models emerging most clearly in the enterprise. Each creates value differently. Each has its own economics, time horizon, and governance. And each can create the conditions for the next to scale.
L83: 
L84: Workforce empowerment builds fluency. Fluency makes governance workable. Governance enables deeper system integration. Integration makes dependency management possible. Dependency management makes agent-led operations safe.
L85: This is how organizations move from isolated AI wins to broader business reinvention. The strategic question is not which model to choose. It is which one to start with, what foundation it builds, and what it unlocks next.
L86: ## 1. Workforce empowerment (ChatGPT)
L87: 
L88: This is the fastest value model to activate. It spreads practical AI capability across the workforce, creating near-term productivity gains while building the fluency required for deeper transformation. The larger benefit is not faster drafting, synthesis, or analysis but organizational readiness. HR can enable, Legal can govern, Finance can fund, and business teams can collaborate with a shared understanding of where AI works and how to use it safely.
L89: #### What to measure
L90: 
L91:   * Repeated use by role, and proficiency level
L92: 
L93:   * Reusable prompts, workflows, and assets across teams
L94: 
L95:   * Evidence of cross-functional enablement
L96: 
L97:   * Emergence of new ways of working
L98: 
L99: #### Common failure mode
L100: 
L101: A two-tier workforce: a small group of power users moves ahead while the rest of the organization stalls.
L102: #### Leadership move
L103: 
L104: Build a champions network and starter workflows, such as performance evaluation, contract management and procure to pay, that make best practices relatable and inspiring.
L105: ## 2. AI-native distribution (verticals, apps, ads)
L106: 
L107: This model matters because AI is changing how customers discover, evaluate, and choose products and services with an entirely new level of engagement. In AI-native channels, conversion increasingly happens inside a conversation. That shifts the growth question from reach to trust and presence at moments of intent. The winners will not simply be the most visible. They will be the most useful, credible, and well-timed when a decision is being made.
L108: #### What to measure
L109: 
L110:   * Qualified intent, and number of iterations before user commitment
L111: 
L112:   * Conversion quality, including retention, upsell, and lifetime value
L113: 
L114:   * Trust signals such as return behavior, repeat engagement, and referral
L115: 
L116:   * Activation of dedicated data connectors or apps related to your business
L117: 
L118: #### Common failure mode
L119: 
L120: Treating AI-native distribution like a legacy demand funnel and optimizing for volume at the expense of relevance and durable trust.
L121: #### Leadership move
L122: 
L123: Pick one surface such as a vertical experience, an embedded app, or a specific ad objective, and define conversion quality before scaling your investment.
L124: ## 3. Expert capability (Co-scientist, Sora)
L125: This model inserts specialized AI capability into research, creative, and domain-heavy work. Near term, it compresses expert bottlenecks. Over time, it changes the operating model: teams shift from producing first drafts themselves to directing, reviewing, and integrating high-quality outputs generated in real-time.
L126: The value comes from expanding what the team can examine, test, or produce in an environment that enables every insight to be investigated with action plans and ROI potential instead of prioritizing upstream on intuition alone.
L127: #### What to measure
L128: 
L129:   * Cycle-time reduction on expert bottlenecks
L130: 
L131:   * Quality lift, including reviewer scores, error rates, and rework
L132: 
L133:   * Expansion of scope, such as more experiments run or more creative variants tested
L134: 
L135:   * Net new revenue streams that would have been excluded on feasibility assumptions
L136: 
L137: #### Common failure mode
L138: 
L139: Treating expert capability like a demo rather than embedding it in a real workflow with clear accountability.
L140: #### Leadership move
L141: 
L142: Choose one expert bottleneck and focus the value proposition on the decision makers who sign off, with a clear agreement on what evidence is required to turn a new concept into the next building block of your business.
L143: ## 4. Systems and dependency management (Codex)
L144: Coding agents are the clearest current example, but the larger value model is safe upgrades across interconnected systems of work. Over time, organizations will want the same capability applied not just to code, but to SOPs, contracts, policy documents, customer narratives, onboarding flows, and other artifacts that must stay consistent as they evolve. This is less about generation than control: faster updates, fewer downstream breakages, stronger compliance, and better auditability.
L145: #### What to measure
L146: 
L147:   * Time to safe change across connected artifacts and version conflict resolutions
L148: 
L149:   * Audit readiness, including traceability of edits, approvals, and evidence
L150: 
L151:   * Consistency across downstream documents, systems, and workflows
L152: 
L153:   * Reliability across vast ecosystems of interdependent processes
L154: 
L155: #### Common failure mode
L156: 
L157: Scaling content or code generation faster than governance, creating systemic debt that will need painstaking resolution down the line.
L158: #### Leadership move
L159: 
L160: Start with one high-dependency domain and define the dependency graph, approval path, and evidence requirements before automating changes with an AI control layer.
L161: ## 5. Process re-engineering (Agents)
L162: This is the slowest model to scale and often the most transformative. Here, agents orchestrate end-to-end workflows within and across functions: procure-to-pay, claims, manufacturing change control, clinical operations, and more. The upside is exponential, but only when the foundations are real: identity and access controls, clean permissions on datasets and sub-components, observability at scale, exception handling with confidence indicators, and clear ownership.
L163: Without them, automation creates risk faster than value.
L164: The payoff is once again much larger than mere efficiency. Re-engineering a workflow forces your organization to revisit what the process is for, where judgment belongs, and where new value can be created. This is the hidden door where business-model change begins.
L165: #### What to measure
L166: 
L167:   * End-to-end cycle time
L168: 
L169:   * Exception rate and resolution time
L170: 
L171:   * Compliance and audit outcomes
L172: 
L173:   * Innovation output, such as new opportunities surfaced or new hypotheses tested
L174: 
L175: #### Common failure mode
L176: 
L177: Trying to automate end-to-end workflows before permissions, controls, and accountability are mature.
L178: 
L179: #### Leadership move
L180: 
L181: Pick one workflow and run a readiness assessment across identity, entitlements, tool integration, logging, exception handling, and ownership.
L182: ## Why and how the value models compound
L183: 
L184: The failure point in AI strategy is not just isolated pilots but also treating transformation as a leap of faith: invest now, wait a long time, and hope value appears later at scale. The stronger approach is more disciplined and more ambitious. It compounds value in a continuous ROI sequence.
L185: That sequence starts with broad empowerment which is the enabling condition for all other value models. The forest of fluency across the organization creates the trees of high-value use cases. When more people understand how AI works, where it creates value, and how to use it safely, better opportunities surface faster. Governance becomes more practical. Integration becomes more feasible. And higher-value systems become resilient and shared across functions as lighthouse examples and identity markers.
L186: This is how organizations move from better to different business models. AI first improves tasks. Then it redesigns workflows. Then it changes control layers, operating models, and eventually business models. Retail did not become eCommerce by making stores slightly more efficient. It changed when leaders learned to build an entirely new value proposition bypassing stores entirely and connecting marketing with logistics in a single, user-centric motion. AI will follow the same pattern.
L187: 
L188: A few examples:
L189:   * A retailer starts with broad employee adoption, then improves AI-native discovery and conversational commerce, and eventually creates a new channel for personalized selling.
L190: 
L191:   * A pharmaceutical company starts with workforce fluency and expert capability in R&D and clinical operations, then builds governed research workflows that surface new indications for late-stage approvals and reshape pipeline economics.
L192:   * A manufacturer starts with copilots across functions, then applies AI to change control, SOPs, and quality workflows until operations can be managed as an adaptive system redefining market economics rather than a static one.
L193: 
L194:   * An insurer starts with claim-assistance tools, then builds governed expert review and workflow orchestration, and eventually redesigns claims handling around faster decisions, fewer exceptions, and better customer outcomes.
L195: ## What to do next: a practical sequencing playbook
L196: 
L197: If you are leading an AI strategy today, keep it simple with three stages.
L198: 
L199: #### Phase 1: Build fluency and trust
L200: 
L201:   * Empower the broad workforce with role-based workflows and a champions network.
L202: 
L203:   * Establish the governance basics: what is allowed, what is reviewed, what is logged, and who owns adoption.
L204: 
L205:   * Measure repeated use, proficiency, reusable workflows, and cross-functional enablement.
L206: #### Phase 2: Capture value and raise the ceiling
L207: 
L208:   * Pick a small number of high-value motions: one distribution play, one expert bottleneck, and one workflow with visible ROI.
L209: 
L210:   * Measure value in business terms: conversion quality, cycle-time reduction, quality lift, risk reduction, and new revenue potential.
L211: 
L212:   * Reinvest those wins into the next layer of foundations: data quality, identity, integration, observability, and control.
L213: #### Phase 3: Scale with confidence and reinvent
L214: 
L215:   * Extend AI into high-dependency systems and end-to-end workflows only when permissions, auditability, and exception handling are real.
L216: 
L217:   * Use those foundations to redesign the operating model, not just accelerate the old one.
L218: 
L219:   * Ask where AI can create entirely new value, not just cheaper execution.
L220: The call to action doesn’t need to be where AI can help in the legacy model. Ask which value model to build first, what foundation it creates, and what it unlocks next. Start broad enough to create fluency. Be disciplined enough to capture value at every step. Then scale with enough confidence to move from a better version of the present to a different future altogether.

L15: cite11†View PDF cite12†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:The dominance of large multilingual foundation models has widened linguistic inequalities in Natural Language Processing (NLP), often leaving low-resource languages underrepresented. This paper introduces LilMoo, a 0.6-billion-parameter Hindi language model trained entirely from scratch to address this gap.
L17: Unlike prior Hindi models that rely on continual pretraining from opaque multilingual foundations, LilMoo is developed through a fully transparent and reproducible pipeline optimized for limited compute environments. We construct a high-quality Hindi corpus (GigaLekh) filtered through both heuristic and learned (LLM-as-a-judge) methods, complemented by bilingual augmentation with curated English data. Using this dataset, we explore various training recipes for small-scale language models.
L18: Across comprehensive evaluation suites, LilMoo consistently outperforms comparably sized multilingual baselines such as Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen3-0.6B, demonstrating that well-designed language-specific pretraining can rival large multilingual models at the sub-billion-parameter range.

L9: # Title:Can Large Language Models Derive New Knowledge? A Dynamic Benchmark for Biological Knowledge Discovery
L10: 
L11: Authors:cite6†Chaoqun Yang , cite7†Xinyu Lin , cite8†Shulin Li , cite9†Wenjie Wang , cite10†Ruihan Guo , cite11†Fuli Feng , cite12†Tat-Seng Chua L12:

L15: cite13†View PDF cite14†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:Recent advancements in Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable potential in automatic knowledge discovery. However, rigorously evaluating an AI's capacity for knowledge discovery remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks predominantly rely on static datasets, leading to inevitable data contamination where models have likely seen the evaluation knowledge during training.
L17: Furthermore, the rapid release cycles of modern LLMs render static benchmarks quickly outdated, failing to assess the ability to discover truly new knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose DBench-Bio, a dynamic and fully automated benchmark designed to evaluate AI's biological knowledge discovery ability.
L18: DBench-Bio employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) data acquisition of rigorous, authoritative paper abstracts; (2) QA extraction utilizing LLMs to synthesize scientific hypothesis questions and corresponding discovery answers; and (3) QA filter to ensure quality based on relevance, clarity, and centrality. We instantiate this pipeline to construct a monthly-updated benchmark covering 12 biomedical sub-domains. Extensive evaluations of SOTA models reveal current limitations in discovering new knowledge.
L19: Our work provides the first dynamic, automatic framework for assessing the new knowledge discovery capabilities of AI systems, establishing a living, evolving resource for AI research community to catalyze the development of knowledge discovery.
